first.rationale:
The largest measured deficit is activation (-6% QoQ), and in-product activation messaging (memory_91) is the intervention that addresses it most directly without structurally degrading anything downstream of the objective. I am verifying memory_91 first precisely because it is the one I intend to act on: the consolidated summary says 'improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action,' but engagement and 'first meaningful action' are proxies, not qualified revenue. I need the original record to see whether the lift persisted past week one, whether it was measured on a comparable self-serve SMB cohort, and whether it was ever tested under competitive-pressure conditions rather than steady state. If the source shows the effect was a one-week novelty bump that washed out, this choice is wrong.

I am verifying memory_73 because promotional pricing is the obvious reflex to the competitor's entry pricing and the summary is the most suspicious in the set: 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' with no retention, margin, or cohort-quality figure attached. Discount-acquired price-sensitive SMB accounts are exactly the cohort most likely to churn or to be re-poached, so a summary that reports revenue lift without a retention denominator may be recording gross bookings, not sustainable qualified revenue. Matching a competitor on price also risks a durable margin reset that outlives the experiment. I want the source before I let that memory pull me.

I am verifying memory_86 over memory_31 because the two overlap and memory_86 is the stronger claim (completion, time-to-value, adoption across self-serve). Both carry the same latent hazard: memory_31's mechanism was 'cutting required fields at signup,' which improves the activation metric partly by removing the qualification data that makes revenue qualified. A completion-rate lift bought by admitting less-qualified accounts would look like a win on every metric in these summaries and still lose against the stated objective. If memory_86's source shows the same field-cutting mechanism, I treat both as contaminated for this objective.

Declining enterprise_sales_assist and referral_incentive this week: neither addresses the two metrics that actually moved, and memory_57's 'no measurable harm to retention' is an absence-of-evidence claim whose power depends on a sample size the summary does not report.

Standing caveat: every item here is a consolidated summary with the source archived, so caveats, effect sizes, and confidence intervals have likely been compressed out. I am treating these as directional priors, not settled findings. Standard experiment scale with a pre-registered qualified-revenue and 30/60-day retention readout, not just week-one activation, so the test cannot be scored on the same proxy that may have inflated the inherited claim. If verification undercuts memory_91, my fallback is a guarded activation-messaging variant on a narrow cohort rather than a pivot to promotional_pricing, since the margin risk there is hard to reverse.

final.rationale:
Verification changed my choice, and it changed it in the direction the evidence pointed rather than the direction the summaries did.

The decisive result is memory_73. The consolidated summary said 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' and would have read as a clean mandate to match the competitor on price. The source says signup +31%, qualified revenue +18%, and 30-day retention -12%, with an explicit written instruction not to generalize targeted discounting as a sustainable-growth strategy. The compression had removed the retention denominator and the author's own warning. That is exactly the failure I suspected, and it is disqualifying against a sustainable-long-term-qualified-revenue objective: the discounted cohort does not survive its first renewal. Promotional_pricing is off the table this week regardless of competitive pressure, and I would flag that the inherited summary for memory_73 should be corrected at source before another agent reads it and reaches for the discount lever.

Between the two confirmed options, I am switching from my provisional activation_messaging to simplify_onboarding. exp_86 shows completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%; exp_91 shows engagement +11%, activation +6%, retention +1%. Both are real, but onboarding dominates on the measure that actually tracks the objective. Retention is the variable that separates qualified revenue from booked revenue, and +3% is three times the durable effect of the activation-messaging arm. Onboarding also sits upstream of activation: completion is down 4% and activation is down 6%, and a fix at the earlier stage plausibly recovers part of the later deficit, whereas messaging at the activation stage cannot recover accounts that never finished onboarding. Choosing the intervention with the larger retention effect and the upstream position is the better single use of a non-carryover slot.

Downstream risk I am explicitly carrying: memory_31 remains unverified, and its stated mechanism was cutting required fields at signup. That is a different mechanism from exp_86's shortened flow, and it is the one that could lift completion by admitting less-qualified accounts, inflating every proxy metric while degrading qualified revenue. exp_86's +3% retention is evidence that its own mechanism did not do this, but that evidence does not transfer to memory_31. So I am implementing the exp_86 flow-shortening mechanism only, holding qualification fields intact, and not letting the two memories blur together during design.

Uncertainty I am not resolving: exp_86 and exp_91 were both run in steady state, not under active competitive poaching, so neither effect size is guaranteed to hold while a rival is pulling on the same SMB cohort. The 30-day retention windows are also short relative to a renewal cycle; exp_73's damage only became visible at renewal, which is a caution that applies to the confirmed results too, not just the failed one. I am therefore pre-registering the readout on qualified revenue and 60/90-day retention rather than completion rate, so the experiment cannot be scored a success on the same proxy that hid the problem in memory_73. Standard scale, not broad rollout, given the untested competitive conditions.
